questions.w1_Q2: Before you brought Fin in, what were the biggest frustrations or limitations with Zendesk and how you were running support? Please describe them in your own words.
questions.w1_Q3: What was happening at your company or within your industry more broadly that may have contributed to your team starting to look at AI agent solutions? If so, please share what those were.
questions.w1_Q4: Was there a specific moment, incident, or event that pushed you from 'this is something we should look at eventually' to 'we need to act on this now'? If so, please describe it.
questions.w1_Q6: Why did you specifically choose Fin over the alternatives you considered? What stood out about Fin?
questions.w1_Q7: Zendesk offers their own AI Agents and Advanced AI as native AI capabilities for customer service. Why didn't you choose Zendesk AI Agents instead of Fin? What about Fin won out over Zendesk's native AI option?
questions.w1_Q9: Now that you've been using Fin for a few months, what is it doing well for your team? Please be specific.
questions.w1_Q10: Where has Fin fallen short of what you expected when you adopted it? What hasn't lived up to the promise?
questions.w1_Q11: How does running Fin on top of Zendesk feel day-to-day? Any friction, integration issues, or surprises about the deployment model itself?
questions.w1_Q13: What would have to be true for you to decide to replatform your entire support stack from Zendesk to Intercom? What conditions, capabilities, or events would push you to make that move?
questions.w2_Q2: What are the biggest frustrations or limitations with Zendesk today? Please describe them in your own words.
questions.w2_Q3: What's happening at your company or within your industry more broadly that may be shaping how you're thinking about your customer support operation? If so, please share what those are.
questions.w2_Q6: In your own words, how would you describe Intercom's Fin AI Agent to a peer at another company? What do you understand it does and how it's positioned?
questions.w2_Q7: What appeals to you about Fin as an option for your team? What aspects sound interesting or valuable?
questions.w2_Q8: What concerns, hesitations, or reservations do you have about Fin? What gives you pause?
questions.w2_Q9: When you think about adopting an AI agent for customer service, how does Fin compare in your mind to Zendesk AI Agents and Zendesk Advanced AI? Which option are you more likely to go with, and why?

v.w1_Q2: The volume problem was real. We were running somewhere around eight to ten thousand tickets a month, and I think about forty percent of those were the same five questions — account verification status, transaction hold explanations, reset flows, that kind of thing. Our agents were burning time on fully repeatable stuff, and that ate into their availability for the genuinely complex cases that actually need a human. That was frustration number one. Number two was that Zendesk's own automation tools, the bots, the triggers — they weren't actually resolving anything. They were routing tickets to the right queue, sure, but the customer still sat there waiting. And honestly, the self-service experience inside Zendesk felt dated. The help center wasn't doing meaningful deflection. We had a knowledge base that nobody was using effectively because the surfacing logic was weak. So between the agent productivity drain and the deflection problem, we were spending more on headcount than the business wanted us to spend.
v.w1_Q3: Our CFO got very focused on the support cost-per-resolution metric in the back half of last year. We had grown headcount pretty aggressively during a volume spike, and when the spike normalized, there was pressure to get costs back down without cutting service quality — which is a harder problem than it sounds in fintech because our regulatory obligations mean we can't just offshore everything or let response times slip. And broadly, I was seeing peers in the industry starting to talk about real deflection numbers from AI agents, not just chatbot-style containment that sends people in circles. That combination — internal cost pressure and credible external signal that the technology had actually matured — made it feel like the right time to move.
v.w1_Q4: There was a board review where our support cost as a percentage of revenue got called out directly. Not in a catastrophic way, but the CFO put a number on the table and said we needed a thirty percent reduction in cost-per-ticket within eighteen months. That was the moment it became a now problem. I had been watching the AI agent space for a while but hadn't pulled the trigger because, coming from sales, I'm skeptical of vendor pitches that overpromise on automation rates. That board conversation gave me the mandate to go actually evaluate it seriously rather than wait for the technology to mature further.
v.w1_Q6: Two things, honestly. First, the resolution rate data from the reference customer I talked to was credible — it wasn't a vendor-quoted number, it was someone I trusted showing me their actual Zendesk reporting. That meant something to me. Second, the deployment model. Fin sitting on top of Zendesk without requiring us to rip and replace anything was a real advantage given how much configuration we had invested in our existing setup. Ada required more custom training upfront, Forethought's pricing model got complicated fast at our volume, and Zendesk's native option had concerns I'll get into. Fin felt like the lowest-risk path to a real outcome in a reasonable timeframe.
v.w1_Q7: I want to be fair here because I went into it thinking the native option would probably win just on simplicity grounds. But when we did a structured comparison, the accuracy on nuanced fintech queries was noticeably weaker in our testing. Things like explaining a hold on an account in a way that doesn't trigger a customer complaint or a regulatory concern — Fin handled those better in our evaluation. There was also a pricing conversation with Zendesk where the Advanced AI tier felt like we were paying for a bundle of features we didn't need to get to the AI agent capability we actually wanted. And I think honestly, there was a strategic concern that if Zendesk's AI turns out to be mediocre, we'd have no leverage to switch because we'd be fully locked into their ecosystem. Keeping Fin separate gave us optionality.
v.w1_Q9: Resolution rate is the headline. We're sitting at around fifty-two percent auto-resolution on the inquiries Fin handles, which tracks closely with what the reference customer had told me. The repeat question categories — verification status, transaction explanations, password resets — those are largely handled without agent involvement now. The quality of the responses on those is genuinely good; we've had almost no escalations from customers who got a bad answer from Fin on the straightforward stuff. Agent morale has actually improved because the queue they're working is more interesting. And the time-to-first-response metric has dropped significantly for the conversations Fin handles, which matters in fintech because customers are anxious when money is involved.
v.w1_Q10: The knowledge base dependency is the main gap. Fin is only as good as what's in your content, and we underestimated how much content work we'd have to do upfront to get it performing well across all our inquiry types. Some of our more complex product areas — our credit product, our business account tier — didn't have clean documentation, and Fin would either escalate or give a vague answer until we got that content in shape. That was a few months of work we hadn't budgeted for. Reporting integration is also imperfect. I'd like to see resolution rates and deflection data flowing cleanly into our existing Zendesk reporting dashboards, but there's some manual reconciliation still happening. It's not a dealbreaker, but it's friction.
v.w1_Q11: Generally workable. The agents adapted faster than I expected. The main friction point is when a conversation that Fin starts gets escalated to an agent — the handoff context is pretty good but not perfect, and occasionally an agent gets a ticket where they have to scroll through the Fin conversation history in one place and the Zendesk ticket in another to get the full picture. It's a two-console problem in a limited sense. Not catastrophic, but it adds a few seconds to every escalated interaction and that adds up at volume.
v.w1_Q13: Three things. First, Intercom would need to demonstrate credible financial services compliance capabilities — SOC 2 is table stakes, but I mean the kind of audit trail and regulatory reporting depth that Zendesk has built over years. Second, our Zendesk contract would need to come up for renewal at a moment when the switching cost math actually works. And third, I'd want to see a peer in financial services at similar scale who has done the full replatform and can walk me through the migration experience honestly. Right now none of those three conditions are met simultaneously.

w1_Q7: Vendor Optionality from Separate AI Layer

v.w1_Q2: The self-service and deflection piece was where we felt the pain most. We had an Einstein bot deployed, and honestly it was barely functional — customers would hit it, get a generic response, and immediately ask for a human. So the bot was adding a step to the experience without adding any value. WISMO — where is my order — was probably forty-five percent of our total volume, and none of that was being handled automatically in any meaningful way. We were staffing humans to answer questions that a decent AI should be able to answer in under thirty seconds. Beyond deflection, I'd also say the reporting on self-service performance was weak. I couldn't easily see containment rates broken down by inquiry type, which made it hard to identify where to invest in content improvements. And the platform licensing cost structure was getting harder to justify to my VP as the team was growing.
v.w1_Q3: We went through a really rough peak season the year before — volume spiked about sixty percent over what we'd planned for, we had to spin up temp agents fast, quality dropped, and CSAT took a hit that took two quarters to recover from. That was the internal catalyst. Leadership came out of that season with a pretty clear mandate that we couldn't keep solving volume problems by throwing headcount at them. At the same time, a few of our direct competitors were publicly talking about AI-driven support improvements, and that created some pressure from our VP to show we had a plan. So it was a combination of the post-peak-season hangover and competitive pressure.
v.w1_Q4: The Q4 post-mortem meeting, honestly. We went line by line through what broke during the peak and the staffing cost overrun was significant — I think we overspent our temp labor budget by about thirty percent. My VP looked at the numbers and said pretty directly that we needed an AI solution live before the following peak season. That gave us a hard deadline, which is kind of what it takes sometimes to move something from the backlog to the top of the priority stack.
v.w1_Q6: Speed to value was the main thing. We had a hard deadline and Fin had the clearest path to getting something useful live in four to six weeks. The ecommerce-specific resolution capabilities — handling order status, returns initiation, exchange flows — were further along out of the box than what we saw with the other options. Ada required more training time to get to equivalent performance, and Agentforce had concerns I'll get into. The Intercom team also moved fast during the sales cycle, which sounds like a small thing but honestly signals a lot about how implementation is going to go.
v.w1_Q7: Agentforce was still pretty new when we were evaluating, and the maturity wasn't where we needed it to be for our timeline. I think the product has potential but we needed something that was going to work well in three months, not six to twelve months. The setup complexity was also higher — it felt like a significant professional services engagement to get Agentforce configured properly for our use case, and we didn't have the internal bandwidth for that project alongside our other peak prep work. Fin felt like it was built to run in parallel with a helpdesk like ours rather than requiring us to rebuild around it. That was the practical reason we went with Fin.
v.w1_Q9: WISMO is basically solved. That inquiry category that was eating forty-five percent of our volume is now handled by Fin at a very high rate — I think we're seeing about sixty percent resolution on order status questions without agent involvement. That alone has freed up meaningful agent capacity. The returns flow also works well; Fin can walk a customer through the return process, confirm eligibility based on order data, and create the return label request. Agents are now handling the edge cases and the emotionally charged situations, which is a better use of their skills. CSAT on Fin-handled conversations is running slightly below human-handled conversations, which I expected, but it's not dramatically lower.
v.w1_Q10: Escalation handling is the main gap for us. When Fin hands off to a human, the transition sometimes feels abrupt to the customer, and we've gotten feedback that customers feel like they're starting over. The context transfer to the Service Cloud case is functional but not seamless — the agent can see what happened but the customer experience of the transition isn't as smooth as I'd like. I also expected more out-of-the-box reporting within Fin itself. The resolution rate data is there, but getting it to join up with our Service Cloud reporting has required more work than I anticipated.
v.w1_Q11: It's mostly fine but there are some rough edges. The data sync between Fin and Service Cloud works, but there's a lag sometimes that causes minor issues — a customer updates their address and Fin is pulling a slightly stale version for a few minutes. That doesn't happen often, but it has created a couple of awkward customer interactions. The agents have adapted well to the two-system reality. I think the surprise was how much ongoing content management work Fin requires to keep performing well — it's not a set-it-and-forget-it tool.
v.w1_Q13: Honestly, the Salesforce dependency would have to break down in some meaningful way — like if the broader company was making a CRM platform change, that would open the door. Or if the Service Cloud licensing costs got to a point where the CFO was asking hard questions about the total cost of ownership and Intercom could make a compelling case on price and functionality combined. I'd also want to see Intercom develop deeper native commerce integrations comparable to what Service Cloud has with Salesforce Commerce Cloud before I could make that argument. Right now the conditions just aren't there.

v.w1_Q2: I think the most honest way to say this is that Service Cloud was excellent at managing human-handled support but not particularly good at reducing the need for humans. And at twenty-thousand-plus tickets a month, that distinction matters a lot. The Einstein bot we had configured — I want to be fair, it was version one of our deployment and maybe we didn't invest enough in training it — but it had a containment rate of something like nine percent, which was basically noise. Customers would type a question, get a response that was either too generic or missed the intent entirely, and then click 'talk to a human' within thirty seconds. We weren't deflecting anything meaningful. The self-service help center was a secondary frustration. We had good documentation — our technical writing team does excellent work — but the surfacing of that content at the point of need wasn't happening. Someone would contact support for an answer that was literally in our knowledge base, and neither the bot nor the help center search was bridging that gap effectively. I'd also flag the content management experience inside Service Cloud as clunky. Keeping knowledge articles current, getting them tied into the bot responses, that workflow was slow and our team was avoiding it because it was so much friction. And honestly, a subtler thing: the agent experience on repeat questions. I could see in our data that the same forty or fifty question types were coming in constantly, and the agents handling them were getting burned out. High performers were asking to move to more complex queues, and I was losing good people to attrition partly because the work wasn't interesting enough.
v.w1_Q3: We're a SaaS company and honestly the internal pressure was coming from the product and engineering culture as much as from the finance side. There was this pretty strong narrative internally that if we weren't deploying AI in a meaningful way in every function, we were falling behind. The CRO — who I report to — was watching what was happening in AI-augmented customer success and support and asking pointed questions about our roadmap. That was one thread. The other thread was genuinely operational. Our product had grown significantly, we had expanded into two new customer segments in the prior eighteen months, and the support volume growth was outpacing the linear headcount model. I couldn't keep hiring one agent for every incremental chunk of tickets. It wasn't economically defensible anymore, and the CRO was asking me to hold the line on headcount while maintaining or improving CSAT. That combination — exec mandate to use AI and an operational need to stop the linear headcount growth — was the real context. I had been watching the AI customer service space for a while and waiting for the technology to get good enough to actually deliver resolution rather than just deflection theater. By the time we started evaluating, I felt like we were past that threshold with some of the newer entrants.
v.w1_Q4: There was a QBR moment that I keep coming back to. We were reviewing the prior quarter's performance and I had a slide showing that thirty-eight percent of our resolved tickets required zero customization — the agent pulled a macro, confirmed an account detail, and closed it. Thirty-eight percent. And we were paying fully loaded support agent costs — salary, benefits, tooling, management overhead — to have humans do that. Our CFO was in the room and she just asked quietly, 'Is this something AI should be handling?' And I said yes, and she said, 'Then let's make it happen.' That conversation took maybe two minutes but it unlocked the budget conversation that had been stalling. Within three weeks we had a formal evaluation underway.
v.w1_Q6: The answer that I keep coming back to is that Fin felt like it had been designed by people who understand what good customer support actually looks and feels like — not just people who understand LLM technology. When we did our pilot testing with real ticket samples from our own data, Fin's responses on complex product questions were coherent and tonally appropriate in a way that mattered to me because our customers are technical and sophisticated. They can tell immediately when a response is hallucinated or generic. Fin held up well on that bar. The no-replatform deployment model was genuinely important too — I wasn't going to recommend pulling Service Cloud out from under the team when Service Cloud was doing the case management job well. And the speed of deployment was real; we were in production in under five weeks from contract signature, which I had honestly expected to take longer. The internal build we had considered got deprioritized because engineering had higher priorities, and Decagon was interesting but had less proven track record at our volume at the time.
v.w1_Q7: I went into the evaluation genuinely open to Agentforce — I had no ideological preference for a non-native option, and I would have happily recommended it if it had won on merit. But there were a few things that shifted the decision. The first was timing and maturity. Agentforce in its current form when we were evaluating was, I think, an honest work in progress. The agentic capabilities that Salesforce was demoing were impressive in controlled scenarios but required a significant amount of Flow configuration and custom development to handle our actual use cases. We didn't have the Salesforce admin bandwidth to build that out in a reasonable timeframe. The second thing was that in our head-to-head testing on a sample of our own tickets, Fin's resolution quality was higher — particularly on multi-step technical questions where the customer needed to be walked through a configuration or troubleshooting process. Agentforce was better at structured transactional tasks but weaker on the open-ended technical support questions that make up a big chunk of our volume. And third — I'll be honest — there was a trust dimension. Salesforce has so many products and the Einstein brand has meant different things at different times. I wasn't fully confident that the Agentforce product was getting the focused investment that Intercom's core product is getting in Fin.
v.w1_Q9: The resolution rate is the headline metric and it's been better than I projected in my business case. We're running at about forty-seven percent auto-resolution on Fin-handled conversations, and when I look at the mix of what's getting resolved, it's not just the simple stuff — Fin is handling a meaningful number of moderately complex product questions where it's walking customers through multi-step processes. That's genuinely impressive compared to what we had before. The agent experience improvement is something I feel good about. The team is working on more interesting problems — integrations questions, escalations with real complexity, customers who need a human touch for reasons that go beyond information retrieval. I've had two agents tell me the work feels more engaging than it did a year ago, and anecdotally retention has been better in the past two quarters. CSAT has held steady overall, which was my primary concern — I was worried that deflecting forty percent of contacts to AI would hurt it, but the customers who go through Fin and get resolved are rating the experience pretty well. The ones who escalate and get a human are also rating well because the humans are fresher and more engaged.
v.w1_Q10: The content dependency is real and I think we underestimated it. Fin's quality is directly correlated with the quality and completeness of the knowledge content it's working from, and getting our documentation into the right shape for Fin to use effectively has been an ongoing project. There are whole areas of our product — particularly around some of our newer features that launched in the last year — where Fin falls back to escalation because the documentation isn't structured in a way that Fin can reliably use. That's partly on us, but it also means the promise of 'deploy in weeks and resolve half your tickets' is more conditional than the pitch sometimes implies. I'd also say the analytics and reporting experience is fragmented in a way that creates real work for me. I want a unified view of resolution rates, CSAT, and case volume that spans Fin and Service Cloud together, and getting that requires some custom work in Tableau that my ops analyst is handling manually right now. And one more thing: the handling of conversations that are partially resolved by Fin and then escalate — the quality of the case summary that gets handed to the agent is good but not always great, and occasionally an agent gets context that's missing something important.
v.w1_Q11: I want to separate two things: what it feels like for the agents versus what it feels like for me operationally. For the agents, the two-console reality is the main friction point. When Fin escalates a conversation to a human, the agent is working in Service Cloud to manage the case but may need to reference the Fin conversation history to understand the context. That cross-referencing adds cognitive load, and while the integration passes the core data through, it's not a truly seamless experience. A few of my more vocal team leads have flagged this as something they'd like to see improved. For me operationally, the friction is mostly around the reporting gap I mentioned and around content governance — keeping the Fin knowledge sources current and aligned with product changes requires a dedicated workflow that we're still building out. What hasn't been a friction point is the underlying technical integration — data is flowing reliably between Fin and Service Cloud, tickets are routing correctly, and we haven't had meaningful downtime or data sync issues in the months we've been live.
v.w1_Q13: A few things would need to converge. First, Intercom's helpdesk would need to match Service Cloud's case management depth for enterprise B2B support — specifically multi-contact case collaboration, native integration with Salesforce CRM data, and the custom workflow logic we've built for our enterprise tier. That's a meaningful product gap today. Second, I'd need a credible migration path — not just technically but operationally. The change management cost of moving a team of sixty-plus agents and years of workflow configuration is real, and I'd need to see that Intercom has helped companies of our size do this successfully. Third, and honestly this might be the most important one — I'd want our Salesforce contract to be at a natural renewal point. We're not in a position to eat termination fees to make a platform switch happen faster. And fourth, I think I'd want the Fin performance to continue or improve — the AI layer is what earns the trust, and if Fin keeps delivering, the case for the full platform follows naturally.

v.w1_Q2: The deflection story was basically nonexistent. We had a Zendesk Guide help center that was reasonably well-maintained, and the Answer Bot had been deployed for a couple of years, but the actual containment rate was embarrassing — something like seven to eight percent of conversations. Customers were clicking through it to get to a human almost instantly. So we were paying for automation infrastructure that wasn't automating anything real. That was the primary frustration. Beyond that, the agent experience on high-volume repeat inquiries was a morale issue. We're a digital media company — our support topics include account access, subscription management, content access problems — and a huge share of those are repetitive. Experienced agents were doing the same work as new hires and that's not a great retention dynamic. I'd also say that Explore, while functional, required more effort than it should to pull insights about where our resolution bottlenecks were. It's not terrible, but it's not intuitive either.
v.w1_Q3: Our subscriber acquisition had grown faster than our support infrastructure, which created a cost problem. And the CRO — who I report to — was very focused on the idea that support should be a retention lever, not just a cost center. But you can't be a retention lever if your agents are buried in password resets and billing questions. There was also a broader narrative in the digital media space about AI-driven personalization and automation that was making its way into the customer experience conversation. And honestly, a competitor in the streaming space had publicly mentioned their AI deflection rates in an earnings call, which got our leadership's attention in a way that internal memos sometimes don't.
v.w1_Q4: We had a two-week stretch where a platform update caused a surge in content access issues — think customers unable to access content they'd paid for. Volume spiked about forty percent above normal and we couldn't staff up fast enough. Response times blew out and CSAT dropped meaningfully. After that incident, the CRO asked me directly what our plan was to handle unplanned volume surges without it being a customer experience crisis every time. That question pushed AI agent evaluation from 'on the roadmap' to 'find the budget and get it done.'
v.w1_Q6: Resolution quality in testing was the deciding factor. We pulled a representative sample of about five hundred real tickets from our recent history and ran them through a blind evaluation. Fin's responses were more accurate and more on-brand than what we got from the other two options. For digital media, tone matters — customers reaching out about subscription issues are sometimes frustrated, and the way the AI handles that emotionally loaded context makes a real difference. Fin did better on that dimension. The deployment speed and the fact that it layered on top of Zendesk without requiring us to change our core workflows were also important factors, but honestly the quality difference in testing is what I put in front of our evaluation committee as the primary recommendation driver.
v.w1_Q7: The native option had two problems for us. First, the performance gap in our testing was clear — Zendesk AI Agents was better than the old Answer Bot but still not at the resolution quality we needed to justify the investment and the change management cost of deploying it broadly. Second, there was a pricing conversation where the Advanced AI tier felt like we were getting bundled into capabilities we hadn't asked for. I've been on Zendesk for years and I have a decent sense of when they're trying to sell me a feature bundle versus when they're solving my actual problem. This felt like the former. Fin solved the specific problem — high-quality AI resolution — more cleanly and at a total cost that was defensible in the business case I had to make internally.
v.w1_Q9: The deflection number is what I care most about and it's tracking well. We're sitting at around forty-four percent auto-resolution on the ticket categories where Fin is deployed — account access, subscription management, basic billing questions. That has meaningfully reduced the load on the human queue. Response time for Fin-handled conversations is essentially instant, which has improved our overall first-response time metric significantly. And the agent queue is higher quality now — the cases that get through to humans are more complex and more interesting, and I've noticed the team is more engaged in how they talk about their work. The feedback loop within Fin for identifying content gaps has also been useful — I can see where Fin is escalating frequently and use that as a signal to improve our knowledge base.
v.w1_Q10: The content gap problem is real. Fin's performance on some of our more niche content categories — specific programming questions, international subscription tiers — is weaker because the documentation isn't as clean or complete. Getting that content into shape has been more work than we built into the project timeline. I also expected the escalation handoff to feel more seamless than it does. When Fin hands off to a Zendesk agent, the case is created and the context is there, but the customer sometimes asks questions the agent would have known from context in a fully human conversation that get missed in the handoff. It's not a dealbreaker but it's noticeable.
v.w1_Q11: Mostly smooth, honestly. The integration is stable and I haven't had meaningful technical issues since the first few weeks when we were still tuning the routing logic. The main day-to-day friction is the split reporting — I want to see a unified view of resolution rates and CSAT in one dashboard and I'm still doing some manual work to get there. The agents have largely adapted to the two-system reality. The surprise was how much ongoing governance the tool requires — you can't deploy it and walk away, it needs regular content review to keep the performance where you want it.
v.w1_Q13: The feature parity gap on case management would have to close — specifically around complex routing logic, our integration with the subscription platform we use, and the reporting depth I rely on for weekly ops reviews. I'd also need a Zendesk contract renewal moment where the switching cost math actually pencils out. And I'd want to see a reference customer in digital media or a comparable high-volume subscription business who has done the full migration and can speak to how it went operationally — not a vendor case study, an actual conversation. Those conditions aren't impossible but they're not imminent either.

v.w1_Q2: I'll give you the full picture because there were a few distinct things. The first and most significant was that our automation was genuinely not automating. We had the old Answer Bot deployed, we had a bunch of triggers and automations doing routing work, but actual resolution — where the customer gets an answer and closes the conversation without talking to a human — that was functionally zero. Every contact landed in the human queue eventually. And at our volume, even though we're not running fifty thousand tickets a month, the cost structure was still problematic because we had over-indexed on headcount relative to what we should have needed for the inquiry types we were seeing. The second thing was what I'd call the macro dependency problem. Our agents were great at pulling macros and getting consistent responses out, but that's still an agent action — it's not autonomous. So we had invested in response consistency without investing in response autonomy. That gap became more visible over time. And the third thing was the escalation path for our Zendesk bot at the time. When customers did interact with Answer Bot and it failed — which was often — the handoff to a human was clunky and customers were frustrated by the time they reached the agent. We were actually making the human interaction harder by having a bot in front of it that wasn't working.
v.w1_Q3: A few things were happening simultaneously and they kind of reinforced each other. We had gone through a leadership change at the VP Operations level — my boss changed — and the incoming VP had a much more aggressive posture toward AI adoption than the prior leader. That created immediate organizational energy around the question. At the same time, the ecommerce space broadly was seeing players claim meaningful deflection and automation gains through AI agents, and there were enough credible case studies circulating by mid last year that it was hard to argue the technology wasn't ready. I'd been watching the space carefully for a couple of years and I'd seen the shift from 'chatbot that frustrates customers' to 'AI agent that actually resolves things,' and I felt like we were past the point where the risk of trying was greater than the risk of staying put. Internally, I had built a model showing that if we could get to thirty-five percent auto-resolution, the payback period on any reasonable AI agent investment was under six months at our volume and headcount cost structure. That model got attention from the incoming VP Operations quickly.
v.w1_Q4: The new VP Operations came in and in one of our first one-on-ones asked me point blank what our AI strategy was for support. I gave him an honest answer — we were watching the space, we hadn't pulled the trigger, we had reservations about previous bot experiences. He listened and then said he wanted a recommendation on his desk within sixty days. That's the kind of deadline that converts interest into action. I had the business case mostly built in my head already, so the sixty-day window was enough to get us through an evaluation, pick a vendor, and get budget approved.
v.w1_Q6: Three things drove the decision. First, the pilot performance. We ran a two-week pilot where Fin processed real incoming conversations in a shadow mode — visible to agents but not customer-facing — and I could evaluate the response quality on our actual inquiry types. The accuracy on order status, return eligibility, shipping exception explanations was noticeably better than what we saw in equivalent testing with Yuma. Second, the knowledge base flexibility. Our product and policy content lives in multiple places — Zendesk Guide, a Confluence wiki, some internal Google Docs — and Fin's ability to ingest from multiple sources without requiring us to consolidate everything into one format first was practically important. Yuma was more rigid about source formatting. Third, I had a reference conversation with the VP of Support at a brand roughly similar to ours in terms of ecommerce volume and ticket complexity, and she was candid about both the wins and the frustrations. That kind of honest reference conversation does more for my confidence than any vendor demo. Those three things together is why Fin won.
v.w1_Q7: I want to be clear that I went into the evaluation genuinely open to the Zendesk native option. Staying native would have been simpler operationally and the pricing would have been more straightforward. But the performance gap in our pilot testing was real and meaningful. Zendesk AI Agents was better than Answer Bot — that's a low bar and it cleared it — but it wasn't reliably resolving the moderately complex inquiries that make up a significant portion of our volume. Things like return exception cases, shipping delay explanations that require pulling fulfillment data, loyalty point questions that have conditions and tiers. The pilot ran for three weeks and the resolution rate was thirty-eight percent on that contact type, which I could verify independently by cross-referencing ticket volume in Zendesk. That independent verification was what I needed. I wasn't going to trust a vendor dashboard number without being able to corroborate it myself. Once I could see that the deflection was real and the customers weren't coming back to reopen tickets, I was willing to expand the deployment. The accuracy on out-of-scope questions was also better than I expected — Fin was more disciplined about escalating when it didn't know something than I anticipated, which matters a lot to me because a wrong answer at scale is a brand problem.
v.w1_Q7: The Answer Bot history was the primary reason I was skeptical of Zendesk AI Agents going in. I had four-plus years of data showing that Zendesk's native AI capabilities had not delivered meaningful deflection for our specific user base and contact mix. The AI Agents product is marketed as a step change from Answer Bot, and maybe it is for some customer profiles, but I wasn't willing to run another eight-month experiment on the native Zendesk option without compelling evidence that something had fundamentally changed under the hood. And when I asked Zendesk for resolution rate data from accounts with our volume profile and contact complexity, the response was not specific enough to move me. Fin gave me a pilot structure that let me test on my own data, and that was more persuasive than any benchmark Zendesk could have put in front of me. The other thing I'll say is that bundling the AI into my existing Zendesk contract would have made it harder to hold anyone accountable for performance. With Fin as a separate vendor, there's a clear performance relationship — if the resolution rate drops below a threshold, I have a contract conversation. v.w1_Q9: The deflection numbers are the headline, and they've held. That's a real capacity story — my team is handling the same human-agent headcount with a meaningfully lower per-agent volume, and response times on agent-handled tickets have improved because the queue is shorter. The accuracy has also been solid. I do a weekly sample review — I pull fifty Fin-resolved conversations and read them — and the quality is consistently good. Fin is appropriately conservative on things it isn't sure about, and the escalation rate on edge cases is higher than I'd optimally want but better than having wrong answers go unescalated. The consistency across high-volume contact types has been strong — subscription management questions, feature access questions, billing inquiry routing — all of those are being handled cleanly.
v.w1_Q10: A few things. The content dependency is higher than I budgeted for in terms of ongoing effort. v.w1_Q11: The two-system model is workable but it's not frictionless. My team is split — the people managing AI performance are working in Intercom, and the people managing agent performance are working in Zendesk. The most concrete friction point is that ticket tagging and categorization doesn't always carry cleanly from Fin's conversation into the Zendesk ticket. It's not catastrophic, but it's the kind of thing that adds noise to reporting and makes me less confident in trend data than I'd like to be. I'll also say the two contracts — paying Zendesk and paying Intercom — creates a procurement overhead that I'd rather not have. It's not a big deal strategically but it's one more renewal to manage.
v.w1_Q13: I'd need three things to line up. First, Intercom's helpdesk functionality would need to match or exceed what I have in Zendesk on the case management and workflow side — not just be adequate, but genuinely better or equivalent, because I'm not willing to trade functional capability for platform elegance. Second, the economics would need to make sense. Right now I'm paying Zendesk and Fin separately, and the combined cost is what it is. For a replatform to make sense, Intercom's full platform pricing would need to either match or beat that combined spend, or deliver enough incremental capability to justify paying more. Third, I'd need our Zendesk contract to be at a natural renewal point. I'm not going to pay an early termination penalty and take on a migration project simultaneously. If those three things aligned — capability parity, favorable economics, contract timing — then it's a conversation worth having. But I need all three, not one or two.

v.w1_Q13: A few things would need to come together. First, I'd want to see Intercom's helpdesk and reporting layer mature to the point where it's not a downgrade from Zendesk's case management infrastructure. Right now I think Intercom is an exceptional AI layer and a competent helpdesk, but I'd need to feel confident it's a strong helpdesk before I'd recommend moving a two-thousand-plus employee company's support infrastructure onto it. Second, the economics would need to be demonstrably favorable — I'd need to show my CEO that the total cost of the Intercom platform is not materially more than Zendesk plus Fin, because the switching cost has to be offset by something. Third, and this is maybe the most important one politically, I'd want Zendesk to give me a reason to leave — a price increase at renewal, a capability regression, a support model change. Right now Zendesk isn't doing anything that's actively pushing me away. v.w1_Q2: Where do I start. So the self-service and automation story in Service Cloud was, honestly, pretty disappointing for us. My VP of Operations was having conversations with our CFO about what the cost-per-resolution trend looked like over the next three years if we kept scaling linearly, and the answer was not a comfortable one. The resolution rate we saw in that trial was forty-seven percent, which was well above what I'd modeled internally as a reasonable expectation. And the quality of the resolutions mattered as much as the rate — I read through a random sample of resolved conversations and the answers were genuinely good. Appropriate tone, accurate information, clean escalations when needed. I came from sales, so I trust what I can actually see over what a vendor tells me in a deck. The pilot data was real evidence.
v.w1_Q7: The native integration argument was appealing — I won't pretend it wasn't. One fewer vendor, everything in one place, agents not switching between tools. But when we ran the same test content through Zendesk AI Agents, the conversation quality wasn't at the same level as Fin. It felt more like an upgraded version of the flow-builder experience than a genuinely conversational AI. For our marketplace use cases — where buyer and seller contacts are often complex and emotionally charged — I needed something that could handle ambiguity gracefully. Fin handled ambiguity much better. The pricing comparison also favored Fin when we looked at the per-resolution model against what Zendesk was quoting for Advanced AI on our seat count.
v.w1_Q9: Resolution rate has held at around forty-five percent, which is consistent with the pilot. The buyer-side contacts are where Fin performs best — transaction confirmations, shipping questions, account access. The more interesting thing is what's happened to my team's engagement. I mentioned morale earlier, and I genuinely think the team feels better about the work they're doing now that the most repetitive contacts are handled by Fin. The contacts that reach humans are more substantive, and I've seen a measurable uptick in CSAT on human-handled tickets. v.w1_Q10: Seller-side contacts are a meaningful gap. Our sellers are more sophisticated users — they ask more complex operational questions, they have higher expectations for specificity, and they get frustrated faster when an AI gives a generic answer. Fin's resolution rate on seller contacts is maybe twenty-two percent, compared to fifty-five-plus on buyer contacts. I kind of expected that gap but it's wider than I hoped. The reporting integration also requires more manual effort than I'd like — I'm pulling data from Intercom and Zendesk separately and stitching it together in a spreadsheet for my weekly review, which feels like a workaround.
v.w1_Q11: Honestly, it's become pretty routine at this point — we've been on it long enough that the team has adapted. The initial friction was the two-console reality, agents learning when they were in Intercom versus when they were in Zendesk and what that meant for workflow. That learning curve was real but it's mostly behind us. The ongoing friction is mostly in reporting — I don't have a single source of truth without manual effort. That's the thing I'd change if I could.
v.w1_Q13: Intercom would need to demonstrate that the full platform can handle the buyer-seller segmentation complexity that's central to how we operate — specifically, different routing logic, different SLA frameworks, and different escalation paths for buyers versus sellers. That's a non-trivial requirement and I haven't seen evidence yet that the platform handles it as well as our Zendesk configuration does. Fin sustaining its performance across a full annual cycle — including whatever our peak season looks like — would also be a prerequisite. And honestly, the internal politics matter: I'd need my CCO firmly on board, because a replatform decision of that scope needs air cover from above me. If all of that aligns at Zendesk renewal time, I'll be making the case.

v.w1_Q2: The self-service story was weak, honestly. We had a Help Center, but the bot experience was kind of embarrassing — it was basically a search widget with a chat wrapper around it. Customers didn't trust it, so they'd just skip it and open a ticket. Our deflection rate was sitting somewhere around twelve percent, which for a digital media platform at our scale is not a number you want to show the CRO. And Zendesk's native AI features at the time felt like they were built to check a checkbox rather than actually solve the problem. I also think there were real gaps in how we were handling repetitive inquiry types — subscription questions, billing stuff, password resets — where we knew the answer every single time but still had a human touching it. That's hard to justify operationally.
v.w1_Q3: I think two things came together at roughly the same time. Internally, we had a headcount conversation that didn't go our way — we requested two additional agents for the back half of the year and got a pretty firm no. So the implicit message was, figure out how to do more with what you have. And then at the industry level, you couldn't go to any vendor briefing or conference without AI agent demos being front and center. I was skeptical, genuinely, because I've seen a lot of technology promises in this space that didn't hold up in production. But the combination of internal pressure and enough peer references from people I actually trust pushed us toward at least evaluating it seriously.
v.w1_Q4: There was a week in Q3 where we had a product release that generated a spike in support volume — nothing catastrophic, but our handle times went up, our queue backed up, and we missed our response SLA for about four days. My CRO brought it up in a revenue sync because it was showing up in churn signals. That conversation made it real. I walked out of that meeting knowing I needed a better answer than "we'll hire more people" when the next spike happens.
v.w1_Q6: Honestly, the accuracy in the sandbox was meaningfully better than what we saw from the alternatives. We ran a set of about two hundred historical inquiries through it during the eval and Fin handled them at a resolution rate that was noticeably higher than Zendesk's own AI. The deployment timeline also mattered — we were told we could be live in a couple of weeks rather than months, and that turned out to be roughly true. I think the pricing model was also a cleaner conversation to have internally because it was tied to resolutions rather than seats, which framed the ROI story in a way that my CRO could engage with.
v.w1_Q7: Zendesk AI felt like a feature addition more than a product. I also had some concerns about whether Zendesk AI would keep pace with the rate of development in this space. Fin felt like a company where AI was the product, not a feature on top of the product.
v.w1_Q9: The deflection on our high-frequency inquiry types is real. Password resets, subscription status questions, basic billing lookups — Fin is handling those consistently and the resolution quality is good enough that we're not seeing a surge in follow-up contacts from customers who Fin touched. Our human agents are noticeably spending more time on the stuff that actually needs a person. I think the containment rate is running somewhere in the low forties percent range, which is a meaningful improvement over where we were.
v.w1_Q10: The knowledge base dependency is real and it caught us a little flat-footed. Fin is only as good as what you feed it, and we had content gaps we didn't fully appreciate until Fin started surfacing them by failing on certain question types. So there was a period of about six weeks where we were in reactive content-building mode that we hadn't budgeted for. I'd also say the handoff experience to a human agent isn't as seamless as I'd hoped — there's some context that doesn't carry cleanly into the Zendesk ticket when Fin escalates, and agents have had to ask customers to re-explain things, which isn't great.
v.w1_Q11: It's manageable but it's not invisible. Agents are effectively working in two environments for reporting and configuration purposes, even if the customer-facing interaction flows through one channel. I spend time in both dashboards, and they don't tell the same story — Zendesk reporting and Fin reporting have to be reconciled manually when I'm building anything for leadership. That friction is real and it adds up over time.
v.w1_Q13: A few things. Fin would need to sustain its performance through at least a full year, including through a high-volume period, not just the baseline months. Intercom's core helpdesk would need to demonstrate that it can match the workflow depth we have in Zendesk today — I'm not willing to trade operational capability for AI novelty. And honestly, the contract timing would need to align. If all of those things converge at renewal, it becomes a real conversation. If they don't all converge, we'll probably extend Zendesk and keep Fin as a layer.

v.w1_Q2: The self-service containment was genuinely poor, and I had the data to prove it. Our Help Center deflection rate was sitting at nine percent over the prior six-month period. Nine percent. For a digital media company with several million subscribers and a very predictable, finite set of inquiry categories — billing, account access, content availability, cancellation flow — there is no world where nine percent is acceptable. Zendesk's guide product and the chat bot they offered were just not capable of closing that gap. I spent a lot of time in late 2023 trying to tune the bot and the results were marginal at best. Beyond the self-service gap, I think there were two other real frustrations. First, the native AI features Zendesk was releasing felt like they were built for the press release, not for production use. I tested their AI-generated reply suggestions with a sample of our ticket types and the quality wasn't something I'd put in front of a customer. Second, my team was spending a disproportionate amount of time on what I call zero-judgment inquiries — questions where the answer is always the same, the agent is essentially a lookup function, and the interaction adds no value to the customer relationship. That's a quality-of-work problem for agents and an efficiency problem for me.
v.w1_Q3: On the internal side, our subscriber base had grown roughly thirty percent over an eighteen-month period and support volume tracked that growth almost linearly. We didn't get a proportional headcount increase — I think we added two FTEs against a volume growth that probably warranted six or seven. So the productivity imperative was real and wasn't going away. At the same time, our VP of Operations was tracking AI deployment stories across other digital subscription businesses, and the question started coming up in our operating reviews: what's our AI story for support? I don't love when questions come in that framing because it can push teams toward deploying something for narrative reasons rather than operational reasons. But I think the organizational pressure, combined with what I was seeing in the self-service data, meant the timing was actually right for once. And honestly, the broader industry context mattered too — our peers at similar-scale digital services companies were starting to report real deflection numbers from AI agents, and those weren't vanity metrics, they were showing up in headcount plans and cost-per-contact benchmarks I could actually verify.
v.w1_Q4: There was a specific data point that did it. We ran a quarterly analysis of ticket distribution by category, which we do every three months, and I saw that sixty-one percent of our inbound volume that quarter fell into five inquiry categories that had deterministic answers. Sixty-one percent. And our handle time on those five categories averaged four minutes and twenty seconds per ticket. When I mapped that to agent hours and then to fully-loaded cost, I had a number I could not un-see. That analysis went into a slide, that slide went into a business case, and the business case created urgency that hadn't existed before. I think having a concrete cost-per-resolution calculation was what converted this from a strategic conversation into an operational priority.
v.w1_Q6: Three things, and I'll give you the data-honest version rather than the sales-pitch version. First, resolution rate in evaluation. We ran a blinded test using six months of historical tickets — a sample of about four hundred — through each vendor's demo environment where that was possible, and Fin's autonomous resolution rate on that sample was the highest. Not by a massive margin over Decagon, but it was consistently better and more importantly it failed more gracefully on the edge cases rather than generating confident wrong answers. Second, time to value was a real differentiator. Fin's deployment architecture meant we were running in a live pilot environment in under three weeks. Forethought had a more involved implementation process that I estimated would take eight to twelve weeks to get to the same point. Third, I genuinely felt like Intercom had built AI as the center of the product, not as an add-on module. That matters to me because I want to be investing in a platform where the AI capability is going to keep improving on a credible roadmap.
v.w1_Q7: The evaluation data made the decision for me. In our blinded historical-ticket test, Zendesk AI Agents resolved a meaningfully lower share of the sample than Fin, and the quality of the resolutions that Zendesk AI did handle was more variable. There were responses generated that I would not have been comfortable sending to a paying subscriber. I also think Zendesk is fundamentally a workflow and ticketing company that is adding AI, whereas Intercom is increasingly an AI company that has workflow and ticketing underneath it. That strategic difference shows up in product quality. And there's an honest vendor trust dimension here too — when I've raised product feedback with Zendesk, the response cycle is slow. The agility I saw from Intercom during the eval process, including how quickly they iterated on a configuration issue we surfaced, was noticeably different.
v.w1_Q9: The containment numbers are tracking ahead of my internal forecast, which is not something I say lightly because I built that forecast conservatively. We're sitting at a thirty-eight percent autonomous resolution rate across all inbound contacts routed to Fin, and for the five highest-volume inquiry categories, it's running in the mid-fifties. That's translating into a measurable reduction in tickets reaching the human queue. My agents are running at a lower volume per day on the repetitive category types, and I can see that in their handle time distribution shifting toward more complex issues. CSAT on Fin-resolved contacts is running about two points below our human-agent CSAT, which is within the range I'd consider acceptable for this stage. The knowledge base surfacing is also better than expected — Fin is actually helping us identify content gaps systematically, which is giving my knowledge management process some useful signal.
v.w1_Q10: A few areas. The escalation handoff is the most significant gap operationally. When Fin hands off to a human agent, the context transfer into the Zendesk ticket is inconsistent — sometimes the conversation summary is clean and useful, sometimes an agent is essentially starting from scratch. I've had agents tell me directly that they occasionally spend the first minute of a handoff interaction re-establishing what Fin already covered, which is exactly the friction I was trying to eliminate. The second gap is around multi-turn conversation complexity. Fin handles single-question, single-answer interactions really well, but when a customer has a compound issue — say, a billing question that also involves an account access problem — the resolution quality drops and handoff rates go up significantly. That's a content and capability issue I didn't fully anticipate. And the reporting integration with Zendesk is not as clean as I'd like. I'm running two separate reporting streams and reconciling them manually for the executive deck, which is not a sustainable workflow.
v.w1_Q11: It's honestly more operationally coherent than I expected, with one persistent exception. The dual-console issue is real. My team leads and I are toggling between Intercom's configuration environment and Zendesk for anything that touches routing, macros, or reporting. It's not catastrophic, but it is a cognitive overhead that compounds over time. The channel handoff mechanics are working adequately — Fin intercepts the contact, attempts resolution, and passes to Zendesk when it escalates. But that seam is visible to agents and occasionally visible to customers. The other thing I'd call out is that knowledge base maintenance is now effectively a shared responsibility across two content surfaces, which we didn't fully plan for in terms of who owns what.
v.w1_Q13: I can give you a fairly specific list. Fin would need to sustain or improve its resolution rate through a full twelve-month cycle, including through our seasonal volume peaks in Q4. Intercom's core helpdesk would need to demonstrate routing and SLA management capabilities that are at least equivalent to what we have in Zendesk today — I'm not willing to regress on operational control. The reporting layer would need to be unified, because running two analytics streams is not something I'm willing to maintain long-term. I'd also want to see at least two or three peer references from companies in the digital subscription space at our scale who have made the full migration successfully. And contract timing matters — if Intercom can offer a transition structure that accounts for the remaining Zendesk contract value, that removes a significant financial friction point from the conversation.

v.w1_Q2: Honestly, the self-service situation was the most pressing thing. In ecommerce, a huge percentage of your inbound volume is order status, return initiation, tracking updates — stuff that theoretically doesn't need a human to touch it. We had a Zendesk Guide Help Center and we'd published a lot of content, but customers weren't using it, and the chat bot experience was so clunky that it was actually generating negative CSAT scores when customers interacted with it. So we had turned the bot down to almost nothing rather than keep running something that was making customers angry. Our deflection was running around eight percent, and all of that was from search, not from bot resolution. Beyond self-service, I think the second real frustration was peak season. Every Q4 we'd hire a bunch of temporary agents, spend three to four weeks onboarding them, and then they'd be gone by February. That cycle is expensive and exhausting and the service quality during onboarding ramp is always inconsistent. I kept thinking there had to be a way to flatten the peak demand curve without just throwing bodies at it.
v.w1_Q3: Peak season was a perennial pain point and that was probably the primary internal driver. Our COO was asking hard questions after Q4 2023 about why our cost-per-contact spiked so dramatically during the holiday period and then dropped again, and what we were doing to structurally address that rather than just riding it out. That conversation was the organizational opening I needed to propose something different. On the industry side, I was seeing a lot of ecommerce peers talking about AI agent deployments, and unlike a lot of technology trend conversations, the specific metrics they were citing — deflection rates, cost-per-contact reductions, peak season handling — were directly applicable to my operation. I don't usually jump on things early, but the use case alignment for ecommerce with AI agents was genuinely compelling enough that I felt comfortable moving faster than I normally would.
v.w1_Q4: The Q4 2023 post-mortem was the moment. We did a detailed cost analysis after the holiday season and the temporary agent spend, including recruiting, onboarding, and quality overhead, came out to something that made my COO's eyes go wide. She asked me directly what the plan was to not repeat that number. And I had been sitting on a rough business case for an AI agent deployment for a couple of months at that point — kind of in draft form, not quite ready to present. That conversation accelerated my timeline significantly. I had a polished version of the business case in front of her within three weeks and we had budget approval before the end of February.
v.w1_Q6: The peer reference was important to get me in the door, but what kept Fin on the shortlist was the deployment simplicity and the out-of-the-box resolution quality. We did a proof of concept over about three weeks where we gave Fin access to our Help Center and our FAQ content, and it was handling order status questions and return initiation at a resolution rate that was genuinely better than what I'd seen Ada demonstrate. The setup process also didn't require a months-long implementation project, which mattered because I had committed to my COO that we'd be live before peak season preparation started. Fin delivered on that timeline. I also liked that it worked on top of Zendesk rather than replacing it, because I wasn't ready to blow up the operational infrastructure we'd built.
v.w1_Q7: I gave Zendesk AI a fair look because the integration story is obviously cleaner when everything is on one platform. But the resolution quality in our test just wasn't there. We ran the same set of sample inquiries through both, and Fin handled a noticeably higher share autonomously, with better response quality on the ones it did handle. I think there's also a product maturity gap — Zendesk AI felt like it was still finding its footing, whereas Fin felt like a more finished product. And practically speaking, I'd heard enough skepticism from other operators about Zendesk AI's accuracy that I wasn't willing to bet our first major AI deployment on it. I wanted something that had enough track record that I wasn't the beta tester.
v.w1_Q9: The peak season performance was the real proof point for me. We went into last Q4 with Fin live, and the temporary agent headcount we hired was about forty percent lower than the prior year for the same volume level. That is a material operational difference and it was exactly what I promised my COO when I made the business case. Beyond that, the routine inquiry handling — order status, where's my package, how do I start a return — is happening at a resolution rate in the mid-fifties percent range for those specific categories. My human agents are spending more time on escalated or emotionally complex situations, which is where they should be spending their time. I'd say the day-to-day morale on the team has also improved because agents are less ground down by the repetitive stuff.
v.w1_Q10: A couple of things. The biggest one is the real-time order data access. Fin can answer questions about return policies and shipping timelines from our Help Center content, but when a customer asks about the specific status of a specific order, Fin has to hand that off to a human because it doesn't have a live connection to our OMS. I knew this going in but I underestimated how much of our order status volume is about specific orders rather than general policy, so the practical containment impact in that category is lower than I projected. I've been working with the Intercom team on expanding the integration layer to address this, but it's not fully solved yet. The second gap is around returns that have complications — damaged items, incorrect products shipped, anything that deviates from the standard return flow. Fin handles the clean cases well but the moment there's any exception logic needed, it escalates, which is probably the right call but does limit the effective containment ceiling.
v.w1_Q11: It's mostly fine but the handoff seam is noticeable. When Fin escalates, the ticket that lands in Zendesk sometimes has good context and sometimes the agent is piecing things together. We've tuned this over the months we've been live and it's better than it was initially, but it's not seamless. My team leads manage two reporting views — one in Intercom for Fin performance and one in Zendesk for the overall support operation — and building anything unified requires manual work. I've gotten used to that workflow but it's not something I'd call efficient.
v.w1_Q13: The integration story is the biggest unlock. If Intercom can demonstrate a native or well-supported connector to Shopify that gives my agents the same order data access they have in Zendesk today, that removes the single biggest technical objection I have. I'd also want to see Fin's OMS integration capability mature enough to handle real-time order lookups, because that's the containment gap I'm dealing with right now. On the commercial side, if Intercom could structure a deal that accounts for the Zendesk contract runway rather than leaving me holding two platform bills, that makes the conversation much easier to have internally. And I'd want to see our peak season handled successfully for a second consecutive year on Fin — one data point is a good sign, two data points is a trend I can build a business case on.

v.w1_Q2: The self-service deflection was essentially nonexistent. We had a knowledge base and an old bot that was rule-based and honestly kind of painful to interact with. Customers figured that out fast and just went straight to live support. With thirty-plus thousand contacts a month, that's a lot of volume landing on human agents that didn't need to. The second thing was the agent experience — Service Cloud is powerful but it's not fast. The UI is dense, there are a lot of clicks to get anywhere, and our newer agents especially were slower than I wanted them to be because the tool has a steep learning curve. Training time and ramp time were longer than they should have been.
v.w1_Q3: We were growing fast — we'd made a couple of acquisitions and the support volume was climbing steeply without a corresponding headcount approval coming through. My VP of Operations was applying pressure to find an efficiency lever that wasn't just hiring. And I came from a revenue and sales background, so I think about unit economics pretty naturally. The math on AI deflection was compelling enough that I wanted to run the experiment, and I had enough organizational credibility to get budget approved without a months-long committee process.
v.w1_Q4: One of our acquired brands had used an AI agent solution at a smaller scale and the team lead there gave me a demo of what they'd seen in terms of deflection. The numbers were specific and credible — not a vendor pitch, just an internal team member walking me through real data. That was the moment I moved from interested to committed. I went from demo to approved business case in about six weeks.
v.w1_Q6: Speed to value was the primary driver. Fin's deployment model got us to a live pilot faster than anything else on the shortlist. The resolution quality on our sample set was also strong — it handled our most common inquiry types accurately and the failure modes were clean escalations rather than wrong answers. I also appreciated that Fin was purpose-built for customer service AI rather than being a feature on top of a broader platform.
v.w1_Q7: Agentforce was still pretty early in its release cycle when we were evaluating, and I couldn't find enough production deployments at our kind of scale to feel confident in it. The demo was impressive but demos are always impressive. I needed to talk to operators who were actually running it in production with real volume, and those references were thin. Fin had a much more developed reference ecosystem and the deployment timeline was faster. I kind of treat Agentforce as something to reassess in twelve to eighteen months when it has more maturity behind it.
v.w1_Q9: The deflection on our top inquiry categories is real and measurable. Order status, return policy, promotion questions — Fin is handling those at a meaningful rate and the CSAT on resolved contacts is acceptable. My human agents are seeing a cleaner queue, meaning the stuff coming to them requires actual judgment rather than being lookup tasks. We've also navigated one seasonal spike already with Fin live, and the volume management was noticeably better than prior cycles.
v.w1_Q10: The data integration with Service Cloud is more limited than I wanted. Fin can handle policy and FAQ-type questions well, but when customers need something that requires accessing their specific account data — order details, loyalty points, return status — there are limitations in what Fin can surface because the real-time data connection to our Salesforce data isn't as deep as I'd hoped. That's capping the containment rate on a meaningful share of our inquiry volume. The handoff context into Service Cloud cases is also inconsistent — agents sometimes get great summaries and sometimes get very little.
v.w1_Q11: It's a two-system reality, which my team has adapted to but which adds friction. Fin reporting lives in Intercom, case and agent reporting lives in Service Cloud, and any unified view requires manual assembly. Routing logic also has to be maintained in two places, which is an operational overhead I didn't fully price in when we made the decision. It's manageable, but it's not invisible.
v.w1_Q13: Honestly, I can't construct a realistic scenario where that happens given our Salesforce dependency. If Intercom built a genuinely deep native integration with the full Salesforce ecosystem — not just Service Cloud but the whole CRM layer — and could demonstrate zero operational regression from a migration, maybe the conversation becomes theoretical. But that's a very high bar and I don't see it happening in any timeframe I'm planning around. The more realistic ask would be deepening the Fin integration with Service Cloud data so the containment ceiling goes up.

v.w1_Q2: The frustrations were concentrated in a few areas that I kept coming back to in every quarterly review. The self-service experience was the most glaring gap. We had a Salesforce Experience Cloud knowledge base that was, I'll be honest, underwhelming. It was structured like a documentation library rather than something customers would naturally navigate to solve a problem. And the bot capability within Service Cloud at that time was essentially rule-based flow logic — you'd build a decision tree, maintain it manually, and the moment a customer asked something that didn't map neatly to a branch in that tree, the bot would either fail or hand off to a human. The result was that our bot containment was essentially decorative. We were deflecting maybe six or seven percent of inbound through self-service, and a meaningful chunk of that was from direct knowledge base search rather than any bot-assisted resolution. So effectively we had a very expensive, beautifully instrumented human support organization handling a large percentage of inquiries that the industry data suggested should be automatable. The second frustration was agent efficiency on the repetitive volume. I came from product where we obsessed over user experience, and watching support agents handle their fifteenth password reset or their twelfth 'how do I add a seat' question of the day was genuinely painful from an experience design standpoint — for the agent and arguably for the customer. The handling was fine but there was zero leverage. Every interaction had the same marginal cost. And the third frustration, which is maybe more operational, was the cost structure. We were running at a cost-per-contact that was higher than our benchmarks for a SaaS company at our ARR tier, and I could see clearly that the primary driver was the ratio of human-to-automated resolution. Service Cloud wasn't giving me a credible path to change that ratio.
v.w1_Q3: There were a few converging forces that made the timing feel right, and I think about them in terms of internal pressure and external signal. Internally, we were in a planning cycle where the CFO had put a pretty firm constraint on headcount growth across the business. Not a freeze exactly, but a clear message that any new headcount needed a very strong productivity ROI case, and support was explicitly called out as an area with automation opportunity. My COO, who I report to, was supportive of the AI exploration but wanted to see a business case with specific unit economics — cost-per-contact projections, payback period, that sort of thing. So there was budget room to invest in an AI tool but the expectation was a measurable operational return. That's actually a comfortable framing for me because it forces rigor rather than just giving you a blank check to experiment. On the external signal side, I was seeing a meaningful shift in how AI in customer support was being discussed in the SaaS operator community. A year and a half ago it was mostly speculative or very early-stage. By the time we were actively evaluating, there were enough documented deployments at companies in our size range and our vertical that I could have real conversations with peers about what the production experience actually looked like rather than relying on vendor claims. That shifted my confidence level. I also think there was a competitive dimension — some of our direct competitors were starting to talk publicly about their AI support investments and I didn't want to be in a position where our customers noticed a capability difference.
v.w1_Q4: There's a story here that I think captures it well. We were doing a quarterly business review with one of our larger customers — a pretty significant ARR account — and their IT administrator raised a complaint about support response times during their peak usage periods. The complaint itself wasn't catastrophic; we were within SLA on their tier. But what struck me was when they said, almost offhand, that one of our competitors they'd evaluated had mentioned having an AI agent that could handle configuration questions instantly at any hour. That comment made it into the meeting notes. It landed on my COO's desk. And the conversation I had with her afterward was basically: what's our answer to this if it comes up again? I didn't have a satisfying answer at the time, and that was uncomfortable for me. I'd been tracking the AI agent space and had opinions but I hadn't moved to action. That conversation was the real forcing function. Within a month I had authorization to run a formal evaluation and a budget envelope to work within.
v.w1_Q6: I'll tell you the story in the way I'd tell it to a peer rather than in the way I'd describe it in a vendor review. We ran a structured evaluation with a shared rubric across all four external options: accuracy on a sample inquiry set, deployment timeline, integration with Service Cloud, pricing model, and reference quality. Fin came out ahead on most of those dimensions. The accuracy test was the most important signal — we used about three hundred historical tickets from our medium-complexity category, the questions that weren't entirely trivial but weren't escalation-worthy either, and Fin resolved them autonomously at a rate that was noticeably higher than Forethought and meaningfully higher than what Agentforce could demonstrate at that stage of its release. The deployment timeline was another differentiator — Fin's team was credible about getting us to a live pilot in under four weeks, and that actually happened. I've been in product long enough to know that a vendor's ability to deliver on an implementation timeline during the sales process is a leading indicator of how they'll operate as a partner post-sale. And the pricing model resonated with my COO — paying per resolution rather than per seat is a natural fit for a cost-reduction business case because the ROI denominator and the cost driver are the same metric.
v.w1_Q7: This is probably the question I have the most nuanced take on because the Agentforce decision wasn't simple. We were genuinely open to it — the integration story with Service Cloud is obviously the most native possible, and our Salesforce account team was making a compelling argument about ecosystem coherence. But when we got into the actual evaluation there were a few things that gave me pause. First, the production reference situation. Agentforce was still fairly new and the references our account team could provide for the specific use case — high-volume SaaS support with complex product questions — were thin.
