The results were genuinely bad — something like eleven percent containment on chat — and it was creating customer friction that was arguably worse than no bot at all, because customers would spend three or four minutes in the bot and then still end up in queue with an elevated frustration level. That left a real mark. The second frustration was the knowledge management workflow. Our product catalog turns over significantly — we do seasonal collections and the content around sizing, materials, care instructions, and return policies changes constantly. Keeping knowledge articles current in Service Cloud required manual effort from our content team and they were perennially behind. Agents were going off-script because the articles didn't reflect reality, and that was showing up in inconsistent customer experiences that I was getting flagged on from my CCO. And the third piece was that our cost per contact was creeping in the wrong direction. We had grown headcount to absorb volume increases but the ratio was not sustainable, and that was a very clear talking point in my quarterly business review conversations with the CCO.
v.w1_Q3: A few things were happening at once. On the industry side, I think the broader retail and e-commerce world had started moving fast on AI customer service — you could not attend a NRF session or read a trade publication without AI in customer service being front-and-center — and we were getting behind the curve relative to some of our competitors who were starting to publicize their deflection rates. That created external competitive pressure that I was able to use internally. Internally, we had come through a challenging holiday season the prior year where support volume had spiked and customer satisfaction had taken a hit. Our NPS in December was notably lower than the prior year and the CCO was very focused on making sure we went into the next holiday period in a stronger operational position. So there was genuine organizational urgency around getting the self-service layer fixed before Q4 rolled around again. v.w1_Q4: Yes. In January, we did a structured post-mortem on the prior holiday season and I presented a slide that showed our cost per contact trend over four quarters alongside our CSAT trend over the same period. v.w1_Q9: It has genuinely performed. Our containment rate is sitting at about forty-two percent of chat volume, which exceeded what I had committed to my CCO in the business case. v.w1_Q11: Day-to-day I would describe it as manageable but not invisible. The case creation sync is generally reliable, though we have had a handful of instances where a resolved Fin conversation did not generate the expected case record in Service Cloud, which matters for our reporting completeness. The bigger operational surprise was how much ongoing content management Fin actually requires. v.w1_Q13: A few things. Third, I would need internal executive sponsorship beyond just my own advocacy, because a full replatform is an IT and finance decision as much as a CX decision, and I am not the only stakeholder in the room. If Intercom had a strong retail reference customer at our scale that I could talk to candidly, that would move things forward. Right now I have Fin proof points, which are useful, but not full-platform proof points for a business like ours.

v.w1_Q2: The self-service gap was the dominant frustration. At sixty thousand plus contacts per month, even a five percent improvement in automated resolution is meaningful in operational terms — that is three thousand contacts per month that do not need agent handling. We had tried to build out Einstein Bots for buyer self-service about eighteen months before I joined and the results were poor. The containment was somewhere around eight percent and the accuracy on dispute-related questions — which is a significant category for a marketplace — was not reliable enough to trust. Beyond the self-service gap, we had a real reporting fragmentation problem. Our operational data lived in Service Cloud, our customer satisfaction data lived in Medallia, our product analytics lived in Mixpanel, and stitching those three together for a coherent picture of the customer experience required a significant data engineering effort. That made our insight cycle slow — typically two to three weeks to produce a meaningful analysis — and in a high-volume marketplace environment, that lag is consequential. And I would add that the cost trajectory was a concern I was already tracking. Our agent headcount had grown at about fifteen percent year over year for the prior two years, and the margin math was not going to work indefinitely.
v.w1_Q3: At the company level, we had closed a Series D about sixteen months ago and with that came a pretty explicit efficiency mandate from the board. The message from our CFO was essentially: the revenue growth we are projecting needs to be accompanied by operational leverage, and customer support is the largest operational cost line that has headroom for productivity improvement. That top-down mandate created urgency that was useful. At the same time, our CCO had been tracking what peer marketplaces were doing with AI — I know at least two comparable-scale marketplace businesses that had deployed AI agents and were publicly discussing deflection results in the forty-to-fifty percent range. We were at essentially zero automated resolution, so the competitive gap was visible. And I think the third factor was that our product team was pushing into new categories — we were expanding into home services and professional services, which have different and more complex support profiles than our core categories — and the prospect of absorbing that complexity with the existing headcount model was not appealing to anyone.
v.w1_Q4: There was a specific board meeting moment. Our CFO presented a five-year cost model for the support organization under two scenarios — linear headcount scaling versus a technology-enabled efficiency scenario — and the gap between the two trajectories was substantial enough that the board asked pointed questions about our AI roadmap. That conversation was reported back to our CCO, who then made AI agent deployment an OKR for Q2 of this year with a specific resolution rate target attached to it. Once it was in the OKR structure with a named target, the evaluation moved from a background workstream to a front-burner project. That board meeting was the catalyst.
v.w1_Q6: On the scoring matrix, Fin came out ahead on three of our highest-weighted criteria: accuracy benchmarking, time-to-value, and reference quality. That gap was decisive in a data-driven evaluation. The reference calls we ran also landed well — I spoke with a director at a peer marketplace who had been live on Fin for about ten months and was candid and positive about the performance trajectory. And the deployment timeline — Intercom's implementation team had us in a staging environment within ten days of contract execution, which compared favorably to the eighteen-to-twenty-four week estimates we were getting from the Agentforce implementation path. For an OKR with a Q2 deadline, that timeline difference was material.
v.w1_Q7: Three factors. First was the accuracy delta — Agentforce scored meaningfully lower on our intent accuracy benchmark, which for a high-volume marketplace is not a trivial difference. At sixty thousand contacts per month, even a ten-point accuracy difference represents thousands of mishandled conversations per month, and that has real CSAT implications. Second was the implementation timeline. The Salesforce implementation partner we spoke with quoted a twenty-week deployment to get Agentforce in production in a way that would meet our functional requirements, which was incompatible with our OKR timeline. Third was our prior Einstein Bot experience, which cast a shadow over the Agentforce pitch in a way that I think is understandable. The Salesforce team was asking us to trust an evolved version of a product that had already underperformed for us. That ask required a higher evidence bar than we were able to clear in the evaluation window.
v.w1_Q9: The headline number is that we are running at thirty-four percent automated resolution on buyer chat volume three months post-launch. That is below our target of forty-five percent but meaningfully above zero, and the trajectory is positive — we were at twenty-two percent in month one. Order status, item-not-received inquiries, basic return and refund policy questions, and account access issues are all being resolved cleanly. The CSAT on Fin-resolved conversations is averaging 4.2 out of 5, which is roughly equivalent to our live agent average for the same inquiry categories, and that parity matters for the internal narrative. I am also seeing real value in the intent analytics — Fin's reporting on resolution rates by topic is giving us a cleaner demand signal than anything we had previously, and I am using that data to prioritize where my knowledge team invests its time.
v.w1_Q10: The gap is primarily in two areas. One is seller-side inquiries. Our initial deployment was scoped to buyer support only, but we tested Fin on a sample of seller questions — things related to payout timing, listing compliance, and performance metrics — and the resolution quality was significantly lower. The seller inquiry types are more complex and more consequential if mishandled, so we have been conservative about expanding to that segment, which constrains our overall deflection upside. The second gap is in dispute and claims handling. When a buyer opens a dispute against a seller, the inquiry has legal and policy implications and requires a sequence of information gathering that Fin does not handle gracefully. It tends to escalate quickly, which is probably the right call, but the escalation hand-off is not well structured — the agent receives a case with minimal context and has to reconstruct the customer's situation from scratch. That is a workflow we need to improve. And honestly, the gap to our forty-five percent target is a KPI exposure that I am managing carefully with my CCO — we are tracking toward it but not there yet.
v.w1_Q11: Functionally stable but operationally imperfect. The data sync between Fin and Service Cloud works, but it is not real-time — there is a perceptible lag in case creation that occasionally causes agents to receive an escalated conversation without the full Fin conversation history already visible in Service Cloud. That happens maybe three to four percent of escalations, which is small in percentage terms but at our volume represents a nontrivial number of customers who experience the friction. The two-console workflow is the most consistent operational feedback I hear from team leads. It is manageable, but it adds training complexity for new agents who are learning two interfaces simultaneously. The reporting fragmentation I mentioned earlier has also persisted — I am still not getting a unified performance view that ties Fin resolution data, Service Cloud case data, and Medallia CSAT data in a single place, which means my weekly operational report still requires manual data assembly.
v.w1_Q13: Specifically: Intercom's full platform would need to demonstrate capability for complex multi-party workflow support — the kind of dispute, claim, and trust-and-safety routing that is fundamental to a marketplace operation. That is not a simple feature addition; it requires a different level of workflow configurability than I currently see in the Intercom product narrative. Second, I would need either a Salesforce contract forcing event or a significant degradation in Salesforce's product or pricing that changed the value equation. Third, we would need reference evidence from a comparable-scale two-sided marketplace that had migrated fully — not just deployed Fin on top — and could speak to how the full platform handled the operational complexity. Without that reference, the risk profile of the migration is too high to bring to the CCO and get approved. And fourth, I would need IT capacity and executive sponsorship, neither of which is available in the current planning cycle.

v.w1_Q2: The frustrations were concentrated in three areas. First was the native AI capability. We were on the Suite Professional tier and had access to Zendesk's AI features, including the answer bot, and the containment on chat was genuinely disappointing — I think our average was somewhere around thirteen percent over the six months before I started the Fin evaluation. The intent matching was weak on creator-side questions, which tend to be more nuanced than subscriber questions, and the bot would frequently surface unhelpful articles and then route to queue anyway. So we were paying for an AI feature that was not meaningfully reducing agent load. The second frustration was content velocity. Our platform ships product updates on a two-week release cycle and our help content was perpetually running behind. The workflow in Zendesk Guide for article updates was not especially fast, and the gap between product reality and documented reality was showing up in agent improvisation and inconsistent customer answers. The third piece was that our ticket volume had been growing at roughly twenty-two percent year over year and we were adding agent headcount at a similar rate, which was becoming a CEO-level concern. I report directly to the CEO and she was asking pointed questions about why our support cost structure was not improving despite product investments in self-service.
v.w1_Q3: We are in a competitive segment of the digital content space and subscriber retention is the primary business metric everything flows through. Our churn data showed that customers who had a negative support experience churned at a rate meaningfully higher than those who had a positive or neutral one — I think the delta was something like fourteen percentage points in twelve-month retention. That business case linkage between support quality and retention was something I had built carefully and it gave me a strong justification for investment. At the same time, our CEO had just returned from a technology conference where she had seen AI customer service demos and had come back with a direct question about why we were not further along. That combination of a retention business case I owned and direct CEO interest was exactly the right environment to move fast. And I will say, I had personally deployed an AI agent at a prior company and I had conviction that the technology was genuinely ready — I was not hedging, I wanted to move.
v.w1_Q4: Pretty specific, actually. We had a platform outage in early Q1 — about four hours of degraded streaming quality — and the support contact spike that followed was significant. We went from roughly eight hundred tickets per day to close to three thousand over a seventy-two-hour window. The queue depth was severe, response times degraded badly, and I had real-time visibility into subscriber churn upticks that correlated directly with the extended wait times. In the post-incident review, the CEO's comment was essentially: we cannot let a four-hour outage generate a five-day support crisis. That framing made the AI agent investment self-evidently urgent. I had an evaluation kicked off within a week.
v.w1_Q6: Three things, in order of importance. Accuracy on our query mix was the most significant factor. I ran a test set of four hundred historical conversations across subscriber and creator inquiry types and Fin's resolution rate was fifty-eight percent — meaningfully above the alternatives, where the next best was forty-one percent. For a high-volume operation where I needed to demonstrate a clear ROI case to the CEO, that accuracy delta translated directly into a compelling business case on agent capacity. Second was the deployment speed. I needed a result I could show in a quarterly business review, and Fin's implementation timeline — we were in production in under three weeks — made that feasible. The alternatives with longer setup cycles would have put my first results past the QBR window, which was a real practical concern. Third was the Zendesk integration story. The fact that Fin was designed to layer over Zendesk without requiring a replatform meant the implementation risk was contained. I was taking a meaningful bet on new AI capability, and I did not want to simultaneously be taking a platform migration risk.
v.w1_Q7: The answer bot history was disqualifying, honestly. We had run Zendesk's answer bot for almost eight months and the best containment we ever achieved was fourteen percent on chat, and that was on the simplest inquiry category. When Zendesk presented their AI Agents offering as the evolved successor to the answer bot, I asked them to show me the architectural differences that would produce materially different results. The demo was good but the production reference data they offered for companies of our scale in digital services was thin. I also looked at the intent and accuracy benchmarking in the documentation and it was not compelling relative to what I was seeing from Fin. I think the honest answer is that Zendesk AI Agents might be a reasonable option for companies who are deeply embedded in the Zendesk ecosystem and want to minimize vendor complexity, but for me, the performance gap was large enough that staying native would have meant accepting significantly worse outcomes. I was not willing to do that, and I had enough decision authority to make the call to go with Fin.
v.w1_Q9: The results are strong and I have the numbers to back that up. We are running at forty-four percent automated resolution on chat volume — that is three months post-launch. Subscriber questions about billing, account access, streaming quality troubleshooting, and cancellation policy are being handled cleanly. Agent-handled ticket volume is down about thirty percent on a per-day basis compared to pre-Fin baseline, and that has allowed me to redeploy two agents from the first-response queue to a dedicated creator support team that was previously understaffed. The CSAT on Fin-resolved tickets is 4.3 out of 5, which is above our pre-Fin agent average of 4.1 for equivalent inquiry types. I presented those numbers to the CEO at the last QBR and the response was positive. The platform outage scenario I described earlier was actually tested — we had a smaller service incident about six weeks after Fin went live, and the volume spike was absorbed without the queue collapse we had experienced previously. That was a meaningful operational proof point.
v.w1_Q10: Creator-side inquiries are the main gap. Our creator support use case involves questions about revenue splits, content ID disputes, promotional eligibility, and payout schedules — these are more policy-intensive and sometimes involve ambiguity in the content itself. Fin's resolution rate on creator inquiries is around eighteen percent, versus forty-eight percent on subscriber inquiries. We knew going in that creator support was more complex, but the gap is larger than I had modeled. The escalation quality on creator conversations is also weaker — the handoff summaries are sometimes thin on the specific context that a creator-side specialist needs. And I would say that the Zendesk reporting integration is something I wish were tighter. Getting Fin's resolution data and my Zendesk ticket data into a single reporting view for the CEO dashboard required more custom work in our data layer than I anticipated. It is working now but it was not plug-and-play.
v.w1_Q11: Generally it has been smoother than I expected, which I say knowing how bad some two-system setups can feel. The ticket creation from Fin into Zendesk is reliable in the large majority of cases. Agents mostly engage with the Zendesk side of the workflow and see Fin as an upstream filter, so the two-console dynamic is less pronounced for us than I think it is for teams where agents are monitoring Fin conversations directly. The main operational surprise was that knowledge base maintenance is a more active discipline than the pre-sale framing implied. Fin performs based on the quality of the content you feed it, and keeping that content fresh at our product release cadence requires genuine investment. I now have a dedicated person spending roughly forty percent of their time on knowledge management for Fin, which was not in our original operating model. That is value-generating work, but it needed to be resourced explicitly.
v.w1_Q13: Specifically: Intercom would need to demonstrate robust voice channel support. We handle a meaningful volume of phone contacts, particularly from older subscriber demographics, and I will not move to a platform that creates a gap there. Second, the reporting layer in Intercom's full platform would need to give me the operational depth I currently get from Zendesk Explore plus the AI-level insights from Fin in a single unified view. That unified reporting is something I keep patching together manually right now and a native solution would be a genuine advantage. Third, I would want to see a clean migration path for our Zendesk ticket history and Guide content — we have years of data in Zendesk and that institutional knowledge has real value. And fourth, pricing at our volume needs to be competitive with our Zendesk total cost of ownership. If those four things are credibly true at the renewal conversation, I am genuinely interested in having a serious migration discussion.

v.w1_Q2: The frustrations were genuine and I had been naming them in my monthly leadership reports for about eighteen months before we acted on them in a significant way. I will walk you through the main ones because they connect to why Fin ultimately made sense. The first was the automation gap. Zendesk's answer bot — which we had configured and attempted to deploy — was genuinely not solving the problem. Our customers are people who are often in a financially stressful situation. Someone calling about a missed payment, or a loan that was declined, or an unexpected fee — those customers are not in a neutral emotional state. And when they come into a chat experience and the bot doesn't understand their question on the first try, or it serves them an article that doesn't answer what they actually need to know, the frustration compounds. We were seeing bot abandonment rates above sixty percent, meaning customers were exiting the bot experience entirely rather than completing it. Some of them then called us — which costs more — and some of them just left without resolution, which is a worse outcome. So the answer bot was not just failing to deflect volume, it was actively creating negative customer experiences. The second frustration was around knowledge currency. I had a customer insights lead on my team whose job was partly to monitor agent response quality, and she was consistently surfacing cases where agents were giving inconsistent answers to the same question. Sometimes that inconsistency was because the agents had different training, but often it was because the Help Center articles they were referencing were outdated or ambiguous. We had a compliance obligation to give consistent answers on certain topic areas — loan terms, APR disclosures, payment deferral policies — and inconsistency in those areas was genuinely worrying. The third frustration was the reporting ceiling. Zendesk Explore is decent for operational metrics but it has a hard ceiling on the depth of customer-level analysis I could do. I wanted to understand, for example, whether customers who had a certain support experience type were more or less likely to expand into additional products. That kind of analysis required exporting data to our data warehouse and running it in dbt and Looker, which was a slow cycle. I felt like I had all this behavioral data trapped in Zendesk that I could not fully activate.
v.w1_Q3: There were layers to this. The most immediate was the business context. I report to our CRO, which is not a typical reporting line for a CX function and it says something about how our leadership thinks about the support relationship — as a revenue-adjacent function, not just a cost center. My CRO had visibility into data showing that customers who had positive support experiences had materially better product expansion rates. Customers who got their issue resolved quickly on first contact converted to our credit-building product at roughly thirty percent higher rates than customers who had a multi-touch, delayed resolution experience. So there was a genuine business case that lived in my CRO's world, not just in the operational metrics. That framing — that better AI-powered support was a revenue initiative, not just an efficiency play — was how I was able to get budget and organizational attention. At the company level, we had also made a deliberate decision that our differentiation in the consumer fintech space was going to be in customer experience. Our rates and products are competitive, but they are not wildly differentiated from peers. Our thesis was that if we could reliably deliver a more empathetic, faster, more accurate support experience, we could earn more loyalty and more referrals than our product alone would generate. That strategic framing made AI agent investment feel like a brand investment, not just an ops investment. And at the industry level, I was watching what was happening across fintech more broadly — I am in a few peer CX communities and the conversations about AI agents had shifted from 'should we explore this' to 'what are your results' over a period of about twelve months. That normalization of AI adoption as a practice made the internal conversation easier.
v.w1_Q4: There was a moment. We had a situation where a batch of customers — probably about four hundred people — received an incorrect communication about their payment due dates because of a system integration issue between our servicing platform and our notification system. They started contacting support in a concentrated window, all asking essentially the same question about a confusing and potentially alarming message they had received. And the interesting thing was that our agents — to their credit — were handling those conversations empathetically and resolving them well. But the volume was high enough and concentrated enough that our queue backed up significantly for about a day and a half, and customers who were contacting us about completely unrelated things experienced a much longer wait than they should have. When I reviewed that incident, I kept thinking: if we had a well-trained AI agent, the payment due date confusion question was actually one that could have been fully resolved without a human, because the answer was consistent and documentable. We handled four hundred conversations with human agents when maybe three hundred of them could have been resolved in seconds. That realization — that the cost of our automation gap was showing up not just in our own metrics but in downstream customer experience for unrelated issues — was the trigger. I put an AI agent evaluation on the Q3 OKR plan within about ten days of that incident.
v.w1_Q6: I want to give you a layered answer because I think the decision had both a rational dimension and an intuitive dimension, and both were real. On the rational side: the accuracy data was compelling. We ran a structured evaluation on a sample set of one hundred and sixty historical customer conversations across five inquiry categories — payment questions, account status, loan term clarifications, complaint escalations, and product eligibility questions. Fin's performance on that test set was the strongest across the field, particularly on the nuanced loan term clarification questions where accuracy matters for compliance reasons. The deployment timeline was also important — we were live in about five weeks from contract signature, which made a meaningful contribution to our Q3 timeline. And the financial services reference cases Intercom provided were credible. I spoke with a VP of CX at a personal finance SaaS company and she gave me a candid forty-five-minute debrief that addressed the questions I actually had, not just the favorable highlights. On the intuitive side — and I know that sounds less rigorous but I think it belongs here — the way Intercom talked about failure modes felt honest. They said directly, 'here are the inquiry types Fin handles well and here are the ones it does not, and here is how escalation works when it reaches its limit.' That candor about edge cases was something I did not get from every vendor and it built trust. In financial services, where the consequences of a wrong AI answer have real customer harm potential, I need to know a vendor understands the stakes.
v.w1_Q7: This is a question I spent real time on because the native path was genuinely appealing in some ways — it would have simplified our vendor landscape and the IT team would have preferred it. The answer bot history I described was the first strike, and I want to be specific about what I mean by that. It was not just that the answer bot had low containment numbers. It was the qualitative nature of what it did wrong. When a customer asked about hardship forbearance options during a difficult financial period and the answer bot served them a generic 'managing your payments' article that didn't actually address their question, that was a customer care failure that I took personally. So the prior experience wasn't just a performance disappointment — it was a signal about the product's ability to understand context and intent in a nuanced way. When Zendesk presented their AI Agents offering and positioned it as a significant evolution, I gave it a fair evaluation. The demos were better. But when I asked for production evidence from comparable companies in consumer lending or personal finance, the reference pool was thin. The companies they cited were running simpler inquiry types on simpler products in categories where the stakes of a wrong answer are lower. For us, accuracy on sensitive financial questions is not just a quality metric — it is a fairness metric and potentially a regulatory one. Fin's grounding approach — staying close to the source content rather than generating freely — gave me more confidence on that dimension than what I saw from Zendesk AI Agents. That was ultimately the decisive factor.
v.w1_Q9: Honestly, the results have given me confidence. We are running at thirty-one percent automated resolution on chat volume, which is well above the near-zero we were achieving with the answer bot. For our use case — remember we are working with customers who are often in some degree of financial stress — the fact that thirty-one percent of those conversations are getting a clean, accurate resolution without a human is meaningful. Payment due date questions, loan balance inquiries, autopay setup questions, referral program details — those categories are being resolved cleanly and consistently. The CSAT on Fin-resolved conversations is averaging 4.4, which I want to highlight is slightly above our human agent average for the same inquiry types. I had genuinely not anticipated that. I had expected parity at best, and the fact that customers who get a Fin resolution are slightly more satisfied than those who get an agent resolution on equivalent queries suggests that speed and consistency are carrying real weight for them. The knowledge gap reporting has also been operationally valuable in a way I did not fully anticipate. My team now has a weekly content review practice built around Fin's unresolved query data, and that practice has actually improved the quality of our overall Help Center in a way that benefits agent performance too, not just Fin. That positive spillover was a genuine surprise.
v.w1_Q10: The most significant gap is in what I would call emotionally complex conversations. When a customer is calling about a hardship situation — they have lost a job, they are going through a divorce, they are asking about what their options are when they cannot make their next payment — those conversations require something that is partly informational but mostly empathetic. Fin handles the informational dimension adequately on those topics. It can surface our hardship policy accurately. But it cannot read the emotional register of the conversation and modulate its response accordingly the way a well-trained human agent can. And in financial services, the way you say something to a customer in distress matters as much as the accuracy of what you say. v.w2_Q9: This is genuinely the central question I'm wrestling with right now, so I'll give you the honest version.
